name: Seljuk Empire
description: The Seljuks were a Turkic ruling dynasty whose conquests connected Iran with a wider empire across western and central Asia. Their courts supported Persian administration, literature, and architecture, while political authority remained divided among rulers, relatives, and regional powers. [s1][s2]

seo.title: Seljuk Empire: Power and Culture in Medieval Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore Seljuk Iran through its regional rulers, Persian literary culture, architectural patronage, and changing political geography.

content.heading: An empire with several centers
content.content:
The Seljuks, also spelled Saljuqs or Seljuqs, brought Turkic dynastic leadership into a political world with established Persian administrative and literary traditions. Their territories crossed modern national borders, so the empire belongs to the histories of Iran and its neighbors together. The Great Seljuks were the principal Iranian branch; other branches governed territories including Anatolia and Kerman. [s1][s2]

Their rise in eastern Iran followed the defeat of the Ghaznavids in 1040. Khorasan—the historical region extending beyond northeastern Iran into neighboring lands—became a foundation of Seljuk power. Its importance continued even when rulers operated farther west. [s3]

content.heading: Persian administration and competing courts
content.content:
The empire was not governed uniformly from a permanent capital. Isfahan and Hamadan were important western centers, while Merv and Nishapur anchored the east. Courts moved, and dynastic decentralization created opportunities for regional patrons. This geography matters: cultural achievement cannot be attributed exclusively to a single sultan or city. [s2]

Iranian viziers, or chief ministers, and secretaries helped sustain government. Persian served administration and much court correspondence, while Arabic remained an important literary language. Writers moved between patrons, and neighboring courts contributed to the same literary environment. The label “Seljuk literature” consequently reaches beyond works commissioned by Seljuk rulers themselves. [s2]

content.heading: Khorasan and the limits of dynastic unity
content.content:
Malik Shah's death in 1092 opened a period of succession conflict. In the east, Sanjar subsequently established a long-lasting center of authority at Merv. His career illustrates how the empire could remain politically consequential even as power shifted between its regions. [s3]

Defeat by the Qara Khitai at Qatwan in 1141 weakened Sanjar's position beyond the Oxus, the river now generally called the Amu Darya. His capture by Oghuz Turkmens in 1153 then destabilized Khorasan itself. These were distinct reversals, not one simultaneous collapse across every Seljuk territory. [s3]

A later endpoint belongs to western Iran: Tekish of the Khwarazmian dynasty defeated and killed the last Great Seljuk sultan, Toghril III, in 1194. [s4]

content.heading: Why Seljuk culture outlasted Seljuk rule
content.content:
Architectural patronage gave this period a durable presence. At Isfahan's congregational mosque, additions associated with rival administrators helped create an influential monument. The four-iwan courtyard, with a vaulted hall opening onto each side, became prominent in mosque design. Madrasas, institutions of higher learning, also received elite support. [s1]

Ceramics from Kashan and metalwork from Khorasan demonstrate innovation beyond monumental buildings. Yet an object described as “Seljuk” need not have been made under a Seljuk sovereign: museums also apply the term to later works continuing the period's artistic traditions. Reading the empire through both political chronology and surviving craftsmanship reveals why its cultural boundaries are broader than its dates of rule. [s1]

content.title: Selected turning points in Seljuk Iran
content.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["1040: Ghaznavid defeat establishes Seljuk power in Khorasan"] -->|"Chronological sequence"| B["1092: Malik Shah dies; succession conflict follows"]
  B -->|"Chronological sequence"| C["1141: Sanjar defeated at Qatwan"]
  C -->|"Chronological sequence"| D["1153: Sanjar captured by Oghuz Turkmens"]
  D -->|"Later western endpoint"| E["1194: Tekish defeats Toghril III"]
```
content.summary: The sequence distinguishes the weakening of eastern Seljuk authority from the later termination of the Great Seljuk line in western Iran. Arrows indicate chronology, not a claim that each event alone caused the next. [s3][s4]

name: Khwarazmian Empire
description: The Khwarazmian Empire grew from a dynasty of Seljuk governors into a major power across Central Asia and Iran. Mongol conquest dismantled its territorial core, although its last ruler continued fighting until his death in 1231. [s1][s3]

seo.title: Khwarazmian Empire: Expansion and Mongol Conquest | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand how the Khwarazmshahs rose from provincial governors to imperial rulers, and why their territorial empire collapsed.

content.heading: A regional title became an imperial name
content.content:
Khwarazm, also called Chorasmia, was a Central Asian region associated with the lower Oxus, now the Amu Darya. It lay beyond modern Iran's borders, but its rulers eventually governed extensive Iranian territories. Gorganj was an important center of the dynasty. [s1]

“Khwarazmshah” meant the ruler of Khwarazm and long predated this particular empire. Earlier Iranian ruling houses had held the title; the later Anushteginid family emerged from the world of Turkic military commanders serving the Seljuks. Distinguishing title, region, and dynasty prevents a misleading impression that every Khwarazmshah belonged to one continuous royal family. [s1]

content.heading: From dependency to expansion
content.content:
The hereditary line began with Qutb al-Din Muhammad's appointment in 1097. Its rulers initially operated under Seljuk supremacy, while relations with the Qara Khitai, a Central Asian imperial power, also constrained their freedom. Independence emerged unevenly through rebellion, tribute, and changing military fortunes. [s2]

Tekish expanded westward, and his son Muhammad, who ruled from 1200 to 1220, inherited an ambitious but contested position. Rivalry with the Ghurids, a dynasty based in the lands of present-day Afghanistan, shaped his early reign. Their forces nearly took Gorganj in 1204. Later Ghurid decline opened opportunities for Khwarazmian expansion. [s3]

content.heading: Military success did not produce secure authority
content.content:
Muhammad's advance into Transoxiana—the lands beyond the Oxus—brought conflict with local rulers as well as former overlords. His sack of Samarkand in 1212 illustrates the violence through which imperial authority was asserted. Expansion should therefore be distinguished from willing integration. [s3]

His western ambitions also brought confrontation with the Abbasid caliph in Baghdad. A march toward Baghdad failed in the winter of 1217–18 amid severe weather in the Zagros Mountains. Meanwhile, danger was growing on the opposite frontier. [s3]

Administration is less securely documented than campaigns. Surviving chancery correspondence suggests continuity with Seljuk practice and the importance of Persian officials. It does not establish how effectively the government operated throughout its territories. [s2]

content.heading: Collapse unfolded in stages
content.content:
The killing of merchants at Otrar in 1218 formed a crucial part of the confrontation with Chinggis Khan. The scholarly account warns that sources disagree over the chronology of early contacts. Mongol armies advanced in 1219 and overran major Transoxianan cities the following year; Muhammad retreated and died in 1220. [s3]

His son Jalal al-Din continued resistance, first retreating toward India and later campaigning in western Iran and neighboring regions. His death in 1231 ended the dynasty's remaining claim to power. The loss of the original imperial core and the end of dynastic resistance were thus separate events. [s2]

Khwarazm itself subsequently fell within different Mongol domains. Its history cannot simply be folded into that of the later Ilkhanate in Iran. This distinction makes the Khwarazmian story a useful bridge between Iranian and Central Asian history. [s1]

content.title: From hereditary governorship to dynastic defeat
content.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["1097: Qutb al-Din Muhammad appointed"] -->|"Chronological sequence"| B["1200: Muhammad succeeds Tekish"]
  B -->|"Chronological sequence"| C["1218: Merchants killed at Otrar"]
  C -->|"Chronological sequence"| D["1219: Mongol invasion begins"]
  D -->|"Chronological sequence"| E["1220: Muhammad dies"]
  E -->|"Resistance continues under Jalal al-Din"| F["1231: Jalal al-Din dies"]
```
content.summary: The timeline separates the dynasty's origins, the conquest of its core territories, and the later end of resistance. It does not reduce the causes of war to one incident. [s2][s3]

name: Ilkhanate
description: The Ilkhanate was a Mongol dynasty governing Iran and neighboring territories from the mid-thirteenth century. Its history combines conquest, continued Mongol political traditions, conversion to Islam, and influential artistic patronage before unified rule disintegrated after Abu Sa'id's death in 1335. [s1][s2]

seo.title: Ilkhanate: Mongol Rule and Cultural Change in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore the Ilkhanate's origins, changing religious politics, artistic exchanges, monumental architecture, and final fragmentation.

content.heading: A Mongol dynasty took shape in Iran
content.content:
The Ilkhanate emerged from Hülegü's mid-thirteenth-century expedition into western Asia. Hülegü was a grandson of Chinggis Khan and brother of Möngke, the Great Khan. His arrival transformed an existing, comparatively loose Mongol presence into a more substantial dynastic establishment. Historians nevertheless debate how far establishing a permanent dynasty formed part of his original instructions. [s1]

The seizure of Baghdad in 1258 ended the Abbasid caliphate there. Ilkhanid power centered in northwestern Iran but extended across neighboring territories, making this a regional empire rather than a state confined to today's Iranian borders. [s2]

content.heading: Conversion changed the court without erasing its past
content.content:
Ghazan's conversion to Islam in 1295 marked a major political and religious transition. Muslim institutions gained royal support, yet Mongol ideas of sovereignty and connections with the Great Khan continued. Conversion should therefore not be described as an instantaneous replacement of one political culture by another. [s1]

Formal rulership also differed from practical control. During Abu Sa'id's early reign, the commander Choban and his family exercised extensive authority across the provinces. The ruler's name at the top of the hierarchy alone does not explain who governed. [s3]

content.heading: New connections reshaped artistic production
content.content:
Conquest and artistic patronage belong to the same history, but they describe different experiences. The Metropolitan Museum identifies intensified exchange with East Asia in manuscript painting and decorative arts. Cloud bands, floral motifs, and new treatments of pictorial space entered an existing Persian and Islamic repertoire. Illustrated books, including copies of the Shahnameh, the Persian Book of Kings, became important vehicles for this experimentation. [s2]

These developments were not confined to one medium. Paper and textiles helped designs circulate, while pottery, metalwork, and architectural decoration offered other surfaces for related visual ideas. The resulting artistic language continued under successor patrons after political unity ended. [s2]

content.heading: Soltaniyeh makes the period tangible
content.content:
The mausoleum of Öljaitü at Soltaniyeh, in Zanjan province, is a surviving expression of Ilkhanid architectural ambition. UNESCO highlights its octagonal form, turquoise-blue dome, and importance in the development of the double-shelled dome in Iran. The monument connects the dynasty's political history with construction techniques and decoration that visitors can still examine. [s4]

Precise construction dates differ between the inspected institutional accounts: UNESCO gives 1302–12, while the Metropolitan Museum gives 1307–13. The broad early-fourteenth-century dating is secure here; the narrower discrepancy remains explicit rather than being silently resolved. [s2][s4]

content.heading: An end to unity, not to cultural influence
content.content:
Abu Sa'id broke Choban's dominance in 1327, demonstrating how personal alliances shaped imperial government. His own death in 1335 was followed by competing claimants and the disintegration of unified rule. [s1][s3]

This explains apparently conflicting end dates. Political histories commonly emphasize 1335, whereas museum accounts may extend the Ilkhanid artistic period into the mid-fourteenth century. A dynasty's political collapse did not terminate its workshops, visual conventions, or influence on later rulers. [s1][s2]

content.title: Conquest, religious transition, and fragmentation
content.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["Mid-thirteenth century: Hülegü establishes dynastic power"] -->|"Chronological sequence"| B["1258: Baghdad captured"]
  B -->|"Chronological sequence"| C["1295: Ghazan converts to Islam"]
  C -->|"Chronological sequence"| D["1327: Choban loses power"]
  D -->|"Chronological sequence"| E["1335: Abu Sa'id dies; unified rule fragments"]
```
content.summary: The sequence identifies selected political and religious turning points. Arrows indicate time order; they do not imply that conversion caused fragmentation or that artistic production ended in 1335. [s1][s2][s3]
